{{Short description|Algebraic structure}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2021}}
In mathematics, for a [[natural number]] <math>n \ge 2</math>, the ''n''th '''Fibonacci group''', denoted <math>F(2,n)</math> or sometimes <math>F(n)</math>, is defined by ''n'' [[generators and relations|generators]] <math>a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n</math> and ''n'' [[generators and relations|relations]]:
* <math>a_1 a_2 = a_3,</math>
* <math>a_2 a_3 = a_4,</math>
* <math>\dots</math>
* <math>a_{n-2} a_{n-1} = a_n,</math>
* <math>a_{n-1}a_n = a_1,</math>
* <math>a_n a_1 = a_2</math>.

These [[group (mathematics)|groups]] were introduced by [[John Conway]] in 1965.

The group <math>F(2,n)</math> is of finite [[order (group theory)|order]] for <math>n=2,3,4,5,7</math> (order 1,8,5,11,29, respectively), and infinite order for <math>n = 6</math> and <math>n \ge 8</math>. 
The infinitude of <math>F(2,9)</math> was proved by computer in 1990.

==Kaplansky's unit conjecture==
{{see also|Kaplansky's conjectures}}

From a group <math>G</math> and a [[field (mathematics)|field]] <math>K</math> (or more generally a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]]), the [[group ring]] <math>K[G]</math> is defined as the set of all finite formal <math>K</math>-linear combinations of elements of <math>G</math> − that is, an element <math>a</math> of <math>K[G]</math> is of the form <math>a = \sum_{g \in G} \lambda_g g</math>, where <math>\lambda_g = 0</math> for all but finitely many <math>g \in G</math> so that the linear combination is finite. The (size of the) ''support'' of an element <math>a = \sum\nolimits_g \lambda_g g</math> in <math>K[G]</math>, denoted <math>|\operatorname{supp} a\,|</math>, is the number of elements <math>g \in G</math> such that <math>\lambda_g \neq 0</math>, i.e. the number of terms in the linear combination. The ring structure of <math>K[G]</math> is the "obvious" one: the linear combinations are added "component-wise", i.e. as <math>\sum\nolimits_g \lambda_g g + \sum\nolimits_g \mu_g g = \sum\nolimits_g (\lambda_g \!+\! \mu_g) g</math>, whose support is also finite, and multiplication is defined by <math>\left(\sum\nolimits_g \lambda_g g\right)\!\!\left(\sum\nolimits_h \mu_h h\right) = \sum\nolimits_{g,h} \lambda_g\mu_h \, gh</math>, whose support is again finite, and which can be written in the form <math>\sum_{x \in G} \nu_x x</math> as <math>\sum_{x \in G}\Bigg(\sum_{g,h \in G \atop gh = x} \lambda_g\mu_h \!\Bigg) x</math>.

''[[Kaplansky's conjectures#Group rings|Kaplansky's unit conjecture]]'' states that given a field <math>K</math> and a [[torsion-free group]] <math>G</math> (a group in which all non-[[identity element|identity]] elements have infinite [[order (group theory)|order]]), the group ring <math>K[G]</math> does not contain any non-trivial [[unit (ring theory)|units]] – that is, if <math>ab = 1</math> in <math>K[G]</math> then <math>a = kg</math> for some <math>k \in K</math> and <math>g \in G</math>. Giles Gardam disproved this [[conjecture]] in February 2021 by providing a [[counterexample]].<ref name="paper">{{cite journal |last1=Gardam |first1=Giles |title=A counterexample to the unit conjecture for group rings |journal=Annals of Mathematics |year=2021 |volume=194 |issue=3 |doi=10.4007/annals.2021.194.3.9 |arxiv=2102.11818 |s2cid=232013430 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Interview with Giles Gardam |url=https://www.uni-muenster.de/MathematicsMuenster/news/artikel/2021-03-04.shtml |publisher=Mathematics Münster, [[University of Münster]] |access-date=10 March 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Klarreich |first1=Erica |title=Mathematician Disproves 80-Year-Old Algebra Conjecture |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/mathematician-disproves-group-algebra-unit-conjecture-20210412/ |publisher=[[Quanta Magazine]] |access-date=13 April 2021}}</ref> He took <math>K = \mathbb{F}_2</math>, the [[finite field]] with two elements, and he took <math>G</math> to be the 6th Fibonacci group <math>F(2,6)</math>. The non-trivial unit <math>\alpha \in \mathbb{F}_2[F(2, 6)]</math> he discovered has <math>|\operatorname{supp} \alpha\,| = |\operatorname{supp} \alpha^{-1}| = 21</math>.<ref name="paper" />

The 6th Fibonacci group <math>F(2,6)</math> has also been variously referred to as the ''Hantzsche-Wendt group'', the ''Passman group'', and the ''Promislow group''.<ref name="paper" /><ref>{{cite web |last1=Gardam |first1=Giles |title=Kaplansky's conjectures |website=[[YouTube]] |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DJEabykk8j8}}</ref>
